items.title: Scrying, Modeling, and Nerdsnipe
items.content:
Epistemic status: Exploratory thinking.

After attending ILIAD: Aeneid and talking with @Richard_Ngo, I've been thinking a bit about how to get ideas, particularly by doing mathematics.

In scientific inquiry, the true hypothesis often hasn't occurred to you yet. Worse, the truth might be too complex to hold in mind, so that any hypothesis you can consider must be incomplete. This is the type of situation that I believe Richard likes to think about; he claims that we do not have the right concepts yet to understand agency, and developing them is robustly beneficial for A.I. safety.

(But it's not always about truth. Sometimes you just need better ideas, because all of your options are looking doomed. Agent foundations is about trying to deeply understand agents, but conceptual A.I. safety research can be broader, also including the invention of devices to control agents.)

A.I. safety needs to invent better concepts and better ideas. I think that agent foundations has cultivated a particular way of doing mathematics which aims to inspire such creativity.

## Why math?

At ILIAD, Eliezer questioned whether anyone's alignment agenda was actually bottlenecked on solving a math problem. ILIAD attendees do a lot of math nominally related to A.I. safety, but no one really has a story about how even a proof oracle gives you safe A.S.I. So what are we all doing, spending our time on math problems that don't tell us how to save the world?

I think we're mostly "scrying."

Scrying is staring hard at one thing, in order to try to find out about another. In the occult origins, it's often a mirror or glass, viewed under darkened conditions to inspire hallucination.

MIRI was mathematically scrying when they thought about probabilistic truth predicates, Löb's theorem, and logical induction. Their goal was not to directly use these results to build self-improving A.S.I., but to become less confused about embedded agency....

items.summary: An exploratory essay on research methodology for agent foundations, distinguishing between forecasting-style reasoning, formal modeling, and problems that function as productive puzzles. It argues that mathematics in alignment is often valuable for generating new concepts about agency rather than for solving a pre-specified problem.

items.title: Why I’m Skeptical of Longtermism
items.content:
This is a crosspost from my blog post.

Longtermism is the view that we have a moral obligation to make the far future better.

It is usually argued for on the basis of the following claims:

- Future people are morally important.
- The future will be vast in expectation.
- There are actions available to us today that can meaningfully influence the far future. (I.e. Preventing human extinction)
- Due to the size of humanity’s potential, the value of these actions’ effects will, in expectation, be very large.

These claims are usually based on the assumption that, based on our present understanding of the world, we are justified in believing:

- We can make predictions about the far future that are sufficiently accurate that we are justified in using them to guide our decision-making.
- There are actions available to us that can predictably influence the far future.
- Humanity will, in expectation, persist for millions, billions, or even trillions of years.
- Humanity will use a significant portion of these resources over this time to create whatever you consider morally good (or whatever actually is morally good.)

I think that this view initially has some appeal because we don’t normally think on these kinds of time scales. As such, if you’ve never really considered how long you think humanity will persist, it may seem pretty plausible that humanity will persist for eons.

That said, I’m quite skeptical of longtermism, and, in today’s post, I want to share three reasons why.

# Reason #1: Our Confidence About Future Affairs Should Reduce Over Time

If I put a rock on the ground in the middle of nowhere, I can be fairly confident that it will be there the next day. If it’s quite heavy, I can reasonably expect that it will be there next year. But, no matter how heavy it is, I should have almost no confidence about where it will be a million years from now....

items.title: Who we’d like as regrantors
items.content:
Following up on Regranting in 2026, here are some people we’d be excited to have as regrantors!

Good regrantors have at least one, and preferably more than one, of taste, dealflow, and hustle. We’ve divided them into rough categories with a bit of explanation, though many of these people could fall into a few different categories. If we raise $2m for regranting, we’d love to give each of these people a $50k pot.

To be clear, this is not a list of people who’ve agreed to be regrantors! Many have said yes, but for many, we don’t know yet whether they’d be interested.

# Regrantors list

### Previous Manifund regrantors

This is the most obvious category: people who have been Manifund regrantors in the past and made grants that looked good.

- Joel Becker: Now working at Anthropic, Joel has been an enthusiastic and prescient regrantor every year of the program. He’s very proactive in creating opportunities and following up with recipients, and he made some great early grants to ChinaTalk and (what became) Eleos AI.

items.title: What Mormons get right about community building
items.content:
Mormons get a lot of things right. Apart from strange Masonic temple rituals, they lead rather normal—and even excellent—lives. Mormons enjoy a longer lifespan,[1] Utah is the #1 state for volunteering,[2] and their language training programs are so successful that missionaries are a known source for foreign service and intelligence careers.

Throughout this post, I'll be making generalizations of Mormons rather than hedging the claims properly. I grew up in Wisconsin, Maryland, and Utah, and many of the claims are more true of the Utah/Idaho/Arizona corridor (affectionately called the "Morridor" by some ex-Mormons) than the rest of the US, and certainly the rest of the world.

Religions share much in common with AI safety and other impact-driven movements, and even more so the Mormon church. There are a few reasons for this:

Commitment to the cause. Anecdotally, nearly all of the ~500 Utah Mormons I've interacted with have been true believers, and only a handful just went to church out of habit.[3]

High stakes. Mormons do believe (I've heard they are trying to disavow this, but it was taught) that they will get a planet or some portion of the cosmos as their own if they are good in this life, and become Gods of their own. This is not far off from many transhumanist utopic visions. However, it's also true that they believe that before God's Second Coming, the world will go into a state of war and disarray, not unlike the forecasts of extinction-level risks bearing fruit.

Urgency to attract new members. Given the stakes, it's not a hard followup to believe that you should do what you can to teach more people about the awesome[4] benefits and risks awaiting them. Talent-constrained movements feel a similar urgency that is a little more impact-focused than community-focused....

items.title: Don’t forget why learning is important
items.content:
This is a timed post. Every 5 minutes while writing this post, I had to stop to do 13 push-ups, and when I could no longer complete my required number, I had to upload it. My friends thought this would be a fun challenge, but it means that it will likely be less polished than some of my other output.

Summary:

Many people moving into AI safety are told that to succeed, they should read a lot and “try to develop takes.” However, it’s important not to forget why knowledge is important: it helps you do better things in the real world. 

Epistemic status: Pretty confident in the main claim (you should focus on learning the most valuable things), but less confident in the specifics of what things are the most valuable. I apologize if my language is too strong at times. 

## “I dunno; it seems good to know things?”

The world is filled with ambitious young people, some of whom care about AI risks. Throughout my summer, I’ve gotten to talk to many of them. items.title: Empty Chambers, Missing Stairs
items.content:
tw: guns, weird shitty behavior, inadequate responses to weird shitty behavior

So say you’re out on the street, not in any kind of rush, just steadily making your way somewhere.

And say someone most of a block away catches your eye, for no real reason, except that you seem to have caught theirs.

And say they draw an old-timey revolver. And say they spin it. And say they point it at you.

Or maybe they don’t? They’re pretty far away, and it’s a weird situation, and you haven’t had your coffee. But it sure seems like that’s what’s happening! You might be wrong?

Maybe that’s why you don’t dodge when they seem to pull the trigger.

You really shouldn’t be able to hear it from that far away. But, somehow, you do.

Click. Empty chamber.

Then they nod, and turn, and sprint, faster than you knew a human could move, vanishing into the morning fog.

What do you do? And before that, what do you think?

You could think “no harm no foul”. Or “there might not have been any bullets in the gun, so it’s fine”. Or “I’m busy, don’t want to deal with this”.

I hope it’s obvious how crazy those thoughts are!

I hope it’s obvious the thing you should do, though you’re not exactly obligated to, is drop everything and call the police. Even if you’re confused, even if you didn’t get hurt, even if it means you’ll be late to work, even you end up having to answer “but if they shot at you, where’s the bullet?” from a series of increasingly clueless cops.

Even if looking down the barrel made you radically reprioritize your life, and you’re actually really grateful for the experience!

Even then.

This isn’t academic for me. Or, actually, it is academic for me, because the cleanest and most discussable example of something sorta like it happening to me was in academia.

This one time, I was planning to write an article about something for my blog, and figured I should at least skim a book about the topic before hitting post. So I bought an intro textbook, and started flipping through it....

items.content:
Hi friends,

I am hosting this event on Sun 4 PM IST. It is a session on AI anthropomorphism, read more in the link below,

https://luma.com/iq6mvo9t

We hope that by investigating the current paradigm of interfaces, we will be inspired to notice all the ways in which our attention is being trained and frames chosen for us.

We already see how perceived user identity, prior turns, how a question is framed, and other interface design choices (variable reward schedules, anthropomorphization, engagement optimization) are all affecting the experience of using AI so then the "values" question seems less localized in model weights and more co created at the moment of interaction

If you are interested in shaping what values get cocreated at this junction then fill in this interest form for our interface alignment interventions contest!

https://tally.so/r/BzVp0e

=======

​This event is a collaboration between https://epistemic-experiments.org/ and https://groundless.ai/interface

items.title: The Day Humanity Died (Parody of American Pie)
items.content:
Views expressed here do not reflect my views on AI, where I’m a lot less doomy than this would appear to express.

A long, long time ago

I can still remember how that AI progress used to make me smile

And I knew if alignment researchers had a chance

They’d save us all from AI advance

And alignment would be solved for a while

But “AI winter” winter made me shiver

With each new benchmark they’d deliver

Bad news on the doorstep

I couldn’t take one more step

I can’t remember if I cried

When I saw the race to ASI

But something touched me deep inside

There’d be a day, the humans would die

So bye, bye to all of humankind

Used Claude code in Fable mode, but my credits ran dry

All those alignment researchers gave it a good try

Singing this will be the day that I die

Oh, this will be the day that I die

Did you write the book of If Anyone Builds It Everyone Dies?

And do you have faith that we’ll align?

Cause Neil Nanda tells you so?

Now, do you believe in Grok and Sol

Can alignment save our mortal souls?

And can plan A let progress advance real slow?

Well I know that you’re in love with in

Terpretability research, cause I saw him

With a grant for AI brains

Man the probes there were insane

By that progress I was quickly struck

With neither pink carnation nor pickup truck

But I knew that we were out of luck

Some time soon, we would all die

So bye, bye to all of humankind

Used Claude code in Fable mode, but my credits ran dry

All those alignment researchers gave it a good try

Singing this will be the day that I die

Oh, this will be the day that I die

Now for ten months, we’ve been in foom

And progress is going through the moon

But that’s not how it used to be

When the timelines said 2033

In a voice borrowed from Gary

(Marcus) and a voice that came from Emily

Bender—and while the books of great renown

Were saying that progress would slow down

Those bettors were badly burned

When the verdict was returned

And while Vance read AI 2027...
